Take the four statements about glucose in turn.
**(a) It is an aldose** ✓ **true.** Glucose is CH₂OH(CHOH)₄CHO, a six-carbon sugar with an
aldehyde group — an **aldohexose**.
**(c) It does not give the 2,4-DNP test** ✓ **true.** In solution glucose exists almost
entirely in the **cyclic hemiacetal** form, with the aldehyde tied up in the ring. Only a
trace of the open-chain form is present at any moment, too little to give the orange
precipitate. (The same cyclic structure explains why glucose gives no Schiff's test and no
bisulphite adduct.)
**(d) On heating with HI it forms n-hexane** ✓ **true.** Prolonged heating with concentrated
HI and red phosphorus removes every oxygen, and the straight six-carbon chain that survives
proves glucose is **unbranched**.
**(b) It is present in the furanose form** ✗ **false** — this is the answer.
Glucose cyclises to a **six-membered** ring, formed when the C-5 hydroxyl attacks the C-1
aldehyde. A six-membered sugar ring is a **pyranose**, named after pyran, so glucose exists
as **glucopyranose**.
A **furanose** is a **five**-membered ring, named after furan, and that is the form taken by
**fructose** — which cyclises through its C-5 hydroxyl onto the C-2 keto group.
So the statement is true of fructose and false of glucose, which is precisely the confusion
the question is testing.
∴ it is present in the furanose form.

With **excess** phenylhydrazine the reaction does not stop at the hydrazone; it goes on to
involve the neighbouring carbon as well.
**Step 1** — one molecule of phenylhydrazine condenses with the **C-1 aldehyde**, giving the
phenylhydrazone.
**Step 2** — a second molecule **oxidises** the adjacent **C-2 hydroxyl** to a keto group
(and is itself reduced to aniline and ammonia).
**Step 3** — a third molecule condenses with that new C-2 carbonyl.
The product is therefore a **bis-phenylhydrazone at C-1 and C-2**, called an **osazone** —
here **glucosazone** ✓, a yellow crystalline solid.
glucose + 3 C₆H₅NHNH₂ ⟶ glucosazone + aniline + NH₃ + 2H₂O
The reaction stops at C-2; it does not continue along the chain, because the osazone is
stabilised by a hydrogen-bonded chelate ring.
Option **(b), the phenylhydrazone**, is what forms with **one** equivalent only — the word
**excess** in the question is what rules it out.
Osazones were historically important because their **crystal shape and melting point** identify
a sugar. They also show something striking: glucose, fructose and mannose give the **same**
osazone, because they differ only at C-1 and C-2, which is exactly where the osazone
obliterates the difference.
Option (c), the oxime, comes from NH₂OH, and (d) glucosamine from replacing an OH by NH₂.
∴ glucosazone.

The **D** and **L** labels are a statement about **configuration**, not about rotation, and
they refer to **one** carbon only.
The convention, due to Fischer, compares the sugar with **glyceraldehyde**. In a Fischer
projection drawn with the carbonyl at the top, you look at the **chiral carbon furthest from
the carbonyl** — the **penultimate** carbon, which for glucose is **C-5**:
**–OH on the right ⟹ D**
**–OH on the left ⟹ L**
So 'D' in D-glucose means the configuration at the **penultimate chiral carbon** is the same
as in D-glyceraldehyde ✓ — option (d).
The other options are the standard confusions:
**(b) dextrorotatory** ✗ This is the commonest error. D refers to configuration, **not**
direction of rotation, which is shown by **(+)** or **(−)**. The two are independent: D-glucose
happens to be (+), but **D-fructose is (−)**, strongly laevorotatory. Rotation can only be
measured, never deduced from the letter.
**(a) configuration at all chiral carbons** ✗ Glucose has **four** chiral centres, C-2 to C-5,
and the letter speaks for C-5 alone. The other three are what distinguish glucose from
galactose and mannose, all of which are equally 'D'.
**(c) that it is a monosaccharide** ✗ Nothing to do with the label.
∴ configuration at the penultimate chiral carbon.

A **reducing sugar** has a **free aldehyde or ketone group** — or can liberate one by opening
its ring — and so reduces Tollens' and Fehling's reagents.
**(a) Galactose** and **(b) Glucose** are **monosaccharides**. Each is a cyclic hemiacetal in
which the ring can open to expose a free –CHO, so both are **reducing** ✓
**(d) Lactose** is a **disaccharide** of galactose and glucose, joined β-1,4 between C-1 of
galactose and **C-4** of glucose. The glucose unit's own **C-1 anomeric carbon is still free**,
so its ring can open and lactose is **reducing** ✓ (This is why milk sugar gives a positive
Fehling's test.)
**(c) Sucrose** ✗ **not reducing** — this is the answer.
Sucrose joins glucose and fructose through **C-1 of glucose and C-2 of fructose**, which are
the anomeric carbons of **both** units. With both tied up in the glycosidic link, **neither**
ring can open, no free carbonyl is ever available, and sucrose reduces nothing.
The general test: a disaccharide is reducing if **at least one** anomeric carbon is free.
Maltose and lactose qualify; sucrose, uniquely among the common disaccharides, does not.
Hydrolysing sucrose destroys the link and the mixture then **does** reduce Fehling's — which
is the standard way of showing that the sugar was sucrose in the first place.
∴ sucrose.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|10|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Sucrose, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, is a **disaccharide**, so hydrolysis must give **two** monosaccharide
units — and in sucrose the two are **different**:
C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O ⟶ **C₆H₁₂O₆ + C₆H₁₂O₆**
 sucrose      **glucose** + **fructose** ✓
So one molecule of sucrose gives **1 molecule of glucose + 1 molecule of fructose** —
option (d).
The two rings are joined by a glycosidic bond between **C-1 of α-glucose** and **C-2 of
β-fructose**. Because that link ties up **both** anomeric carbons, sucrose is a **non-reducing**
sugar, and hydrolysing it frees both.
The reaction is called **inversion**, and the product mixture **invert sugar**. Sucrose itself
is dextrorotatory, [α] = +66·5°; after hydrolysis the mixture becomes **laevorotatory**,
because glucose at +52·5° is outweighed by fructose at −92·4°. The sign of the rotation
inverts, which is where the name comes from.
Option (a), two glucose molecules, would describe **maltose**; option (c) cannot be right
because three hexose units would need a trisaccharide.
∴ 1 molecule of glucose + 1 molecule of fructose.

Note: the printed key gives (a). Sucrose is made of one glucose and one fructose unit, not
two glucoses, so the key is wrong and has been corrected to (d).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|11|Pradeep Chemistry:
An **aldose** has an aldehyde group and a **ketose** a keto group, so the question asks which
disaccharide is built from **one of each**.
**(a) Sucrose** ✓ — hydrolyses to **glucose (an aldohexose) + fructose (a ketohexose)**. One
aldose and one ketose, exactly as required ✓
**(b) Maltose** ✗ — hydrolyses to **two molecules of glucose**, so two aldoses.
**(c) Lactose** ✗ — hydrolyses to **glucose + galactose**, both **aldoses**.
So (d) 'all the three' fails as well.
Sucrose is the odd one out among the three common disaccharides in more ways than this, and
they are connected. Because fructose is a **ketose**, its anomeric carbon is **C-2** rather
than C-1, and the glycosidic bond in sucrose runs from glucose C-1 to fructose **C-2** —
tying up the anomeric carbon of both units. That is why sucrose alone among the three is
**non-reducing**, and why it alone shows **inversion** on hydrolysis.
A useful way to keep the three straight:
**maltose** = glucose + glucose (α-1,4), reducing
**lactose** = galactose + glucose (β-1,4), reducing
**sucrose** = glucose + fructose (α-1,β-2), **non-reducing**
∴ sucrose.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|12|Pradeep Chemistry:
The sugar of milk is **lactose** ✓, which is why it is called **milk sugar**. Cow's milk
contains about **4–5 %** lactose and human milk about 7 %.
Its structure: **galactose joined to glucose** by a **β-1,4** glycosidic link, from C-1 of
galactose to C-4 of glucose. The glucose unit's anomeric carbon is left free, so lactose is a
**reducing** sugar and gives a positive Fehling's test.
The others belong elsewhere:
**(a) Sucrose** — cane and beet sugar, the ordinary table sugar, from plants.
**(b) Maltose** — malt sugar, formed when starch is partly hydrolysed, as in germinating
barley.
**(d) Cellulose** — not a disaccharide at all but a **polysaccharide**, the structural
material of plant cell walls.
The **β** link is worth noting because it has consequences people meet directly. Digesting
lactose requires the enzyme **lactase**, which many adults stop producing; the undigested
sugar is then fermented by gut bacteria, which is **lactose intolerance**. The same β-linkage
problem on a larger scale is why humans cannot digest cellulose at all.
∴ lactose.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|13|Pradeep Chemistry:
Lactose is a **disaccharide** made of **two different** monosaccharide units, joined by a
β-1,4 glycosidic bond between C-1 of galactose and C-4 of glucose. Hydrolysis breaks that
bond and releases both:
lactose + H₂O --(lactase, or dilute acid)--> **glucose + galactose** ✓
The two products are **C-4 epimers** — identical in every respect except the orientation of
the hydroxyl at carbon 4 — which is why they are so easily confused and why the question is
worth asking.
The other options belong to the other common disaccharides:
**(a) glucose and glucose** — that is **maltose**, joined α-1,4
**(b) glucose and fructose** — that is **sucrose**, joined α-1,β-2
The hydrolysis has a familiar practical side. The enzyme **lactase** performs it in the small
intestine, and where lactase is absent the lactose passes undigested into the colon, where
bacteria ferment it — the cause of lactose intolerance. Commercial 'lactose-free' milk is
simply milk in which this hydrolysis has already been carried out, which is also why it
tastes slightly sweeter: glucose and galactose are sweeter than lactose itself.
∴ glucose and galactose.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|14|Pradeep Chemistry:
The hydrolysis of sucrose is called **inversion** ✓, and the mixture of products is called
**invert sugar**.
The name records what happens to the **optical rotation**:
**before** hydrolysis — sucrose is **dextrorotatory**, [α] = **+66·5°**
**after** hydrolysis — the equimolar mixture is **laevorotatory**, [α] ≈ **−20°**
because glucose at **+52·5°** is outweighed by fructose at **−92·4°**
The sign of the rotation therefore **inverts**, from + to −, as the reaction proceeds. That
inversion is what gives the process its name, and because it can be followed continuously in
a polarimeter, it became one of the classic reactions for studying **reaction kinetics**. (It
is a textbook pseudo-first-order reaction, since the water is in vast excess.)
The enzyme that catalyses it is accordingly named **invertase**.
Why the others are wrong:
**(c) hydrolysis** is literally what the reaction is, but the question asks what the process
is **called** — and it has a specific name, which is the point of the question.
**(a) esterification** forms an ester from an acid and an alcohol.
**(b) saponification** is the alkaline hydrolysis of a fat to soap.
Invert sugar is sweeter than sucrose and does not crystallise readily, which is why honey —
naturally rich in it — stays liquid.
∴ inversion.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|15|Pradeep Chemistry:
All four options are polymers of glucose (except that one is the monomer), so the question is
where each is found.
**(b) Glycogen** ✓ — the storage polysaccharide of **animals**, held in the **liver** and the
muscles, and often called **animal starch**.
The others are all from plants, or are not stores at all:
**(a) Amylose** — the unbranched, helical fraction of **starch**, stored in plants
**(c) Amylopectin** — the branched fraction of **starch**, again stored in plants
**(d) Cellulose** — the **structural** material of plant cell walls, never a food store
Glycogen's structure fits its job precisely. It is an α-1,4 chain with **α-1,6 branch points
about every ten residues**, far more heavily branched than amylopectin's one in twenty-five.
All those branch ends give the degrading enzymes many places to attack at once, so glucose
can be released **quickly** when blood sugar falls — which is exactly what an animal needs
between meals or during exertion.
The adult human liver stores roughly **100 g** of glycogen, enough to hold blood glucose
steady for about a day of fasting, with another 400 g in the muscles for local use.
Plants, being stationary and slow, can afford the less branched starch.
∴ glycogen.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|16|Pradeep Chemistry:
The important constituent of the **plant cell wall** is **cellulose** ✓ — it is the most
abundant organic compound on Earth, making up about half of all plant material and nearly
90 % of cotton fibre.
Cellulose is a straight-chain polysaccharide of **glucose joined by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds**.
That **β** linkage is what makes it structural rather than nutritional:
the β geometry lets each successive glucose unit **flip 180°**, so the chain lies out
**straight** instead of coiling
straight chains pack side by side, held together by extensive **hydrogen bonding** between
the many hydroxyl groups
the result is rigid, insoluble **fibres** of great tensile strength — exactly what a cell
wall needs
Contrast **starch**, built of the same glucose but with **α-1,4** links, which force the chain
into a helix that cannot pack and is easily digested.
The other options are wrong by function: **(a) lipids** form the cell **membrane**, not the
wall; **(c) proteins** are structural and catalytic within the cell; **(d) vitamins** are
micronutrients, present in traces.
Humans cannot digest cellulose, lacking the enzyme **cellulase** to break β-1,4 bonds, which
is why it passes through as dietary fibre — while cattle manage it only through the bacteria
in their rumen.
∴ cellulose.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|17|Pradeep Chemistry:
Amino acids that the body **cannot synthesise** and must obtain from food are called
**essential amino acids** ✓ — the word 'essential' means essential **in the diet**, not
essential to life, since all twenty are that.
There are **ten** of them for humans: valine, leucine, isoleucine, threonine, methionine,
phenylalanine, tryptophan, lysine, histidine and arginine (the last two being needed
especially during growth).
The remaining ten are **non-essential** — option (d) — meaning the body can make them from
other compounds, so they need not appear in the diet.
Options (a) and (c), acidic and basic amino acids, classify by the **side chain** instead:
**acidic** — aspartic and glutamic acid, with an extra –COOH
**basic** — lysine, arginine and histidine, with an extra amino group
**neutral** — all the rest
That is a quite separate classification, and the two overlap: lysine, for instance, is both
basic and essential.
The dietary consequence matters. A protein containing all the essential amino acids in
adequate amounts is a **complete** protein — egg, milk and meat are examples — while most
single plant proteins are deficient in one or two. Cereals are low in **lysine** and pulses
low in **methionine**, which is why the traditional combination of rice or wheat with dal
supplies between them what neither does alone.
∴ essential amino acids.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|23|Pradeep Chemistry:
The **secondary** structure of a protein — the α-helix and the β-pleated sheet — is held
together by **hydrogen bonds** ✓.
The hydrogen bonds form between the **backbone** groups of the peptide chain:
the **>C=O** of one peptide link acts as acceptor
the **>N–H** of another acts as donor
**In the α-helix** the bond runs from the C=O of residue *n* to the N–H of residue *n + 4*,
within the **same** chain. That spacing is what gives the helix its 3·6 residues per turn and
its 5·4 Å pitch.
**In the β-pleated sheet** the bonds run **between** neighbouring stretches of chain lying
side by side, holding the sheet flat.
Individually a hydrogen bond is weak, about 20 kJ mol⁻¹, but a protein has thousands of them
and their combined effect is what maintains the shape.
Why not the others:
**(a) Peptide bonds** ✗ — these are the **covalent** C–N links that join the amino acids into
a chain. They define the **primary** structure; they do not hold the chain in a shape.
**(b) van der Waals forces** and **(d) dipole-dipole interactions** ✗ — present, but far too
weak to be the organising force.
Breaking those hydrogen bonds by heat or acid is exactly what **denaturation** is: the helix
unwinds, the protein loses its shape and its function, and an egg white turns solid.
∴ hydrogen bonds.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|24|Pradeep Chemistry:
Digestion breaks a protein down in stages, and the question asks where it **ends**.
The sequence is
**protein ⟶ proteoses ⟶ peptones ⟶ polypeptides ⟶ peptides ⟶ α-amino acids** ✓
Each step hydrolyses more of the **peptide (–CO–NH–) bonds**, and the process stops only when
every one has gone and the chain has been reduced to its individual building blocks, the
**α-amino acids** — option (d).
The enzymes that do it work in turn: **pepsin** in the acid of the stomach, then **trypsin**
and **chymotrypsin** from the pancreas, and finally the **peptidases** of the intestinal wall,
which remove the last amino acids one at a time.
The reason digestion must go all the way is that only **free amino acids** are small enough to
be absorbed through the intestinal wall into the blood. The body then reassembles them into
its own proteins in whatever order its DNA specifies.
The other options are all **intermediate** stages, and they are offered in the order they
appear: (b) peptones and (c) proteoses come early, (a) peptides come late — but none of them
is the end.
The amino acids are α-amino acids because the –NH₂ sits on the carbon **adjacent** to the
–COOH, which is the arrangement found in every protein.
∴ α-amino acids.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|25|Pradeep Chemistry:
A **peptide bond** is the **–CO–NH–** link formed when the –COOH of one amino acid condenses
with the –NH₂ of the next, losing water:
H₂N–CHR–COOH + H₂N–CHR′–COOH ⟶ H₂N–CHR–**CO–NH**–CHR′–COOH + H₂O
It is therefore the defining feature of **proteins** ✓ — long chains of amino acids joined
this way, the sequence of which is a protein's **primary structure**.
The other options are built from quite different linkages, which is the point of the
question:
**(a) Polysaccharides** — joined by **glycosidic** bonds, C–O–C links between sugar units
**(c) Nucleotides** — assembled into nucleic acids by **phosphodiester** bonds between the
sugar and phosphate groups
**(b) Vitamins** — not polymers at all, but small individual molecules of many different
kinds
The peptide bond has one property worth knowing: it is **planar and rigid**, because the
nitrogen lone pair delocalises into the carbonyl, giving the C–N bond partial double-bond
character. There is no free rotation about it, and that rigidity is what makes the regular
α-helix and β-sheet possible at all.
Chemically the peptide bond is simply an **amide**, which is why proteins are hydrolysed by
the same acids, bases and enzymes that hydrolyse any amide.
∴ proteins.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|26|Pradeep Chemistry:
Insulin contains **three** disulphide linkages ✓ — the answer is (a).
The molecule is built from **two polypeptide chains**:
chain **A**, 21 amino acid residues
chain **B**, 30 residues
and the three **–S–S–** bridges, formed by oxidation of pairs of cysteine –SH groups, are
arranged as:
**two interchain** bridges, holding chain A to chain B
**one intrachain** bridge, within chain A alone
Those three bonds are what hold the two chains together as a single functional hormone. Cut
them — by reduction — and the chains fall apart and the hormone loses all activity, which is
the standard demonstration that **tertiary structure determines function**.
Disulphide bridges are **covalent**, so they are much stronger than the hydrogen bonds that
shape the secondary structure, and they are what make a protein's folded shape permanent
rather than merely stable.
Insulin matters historically as well: it was the **first protein whose complete amino acid
sequence was determined**, by Frederick Sanger in 1955, work that required him to locate
exactly these three bridges, and the **first to be synthesised** and the first made by
recombinant DNA.
The same kind of bridge, on a larger scale, is what gives hair and wool their strength — and
breaking and reforming the disulphide bonds in keratin is how hair is permanently waved.
∴ 3.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|27|Pradeep Chemistry:
Antibodies, also called **immunoglobulins**, are **proteins** ✓ — large, Y-shaped molecules
produced by the B-lymphocytes of the immune system.
Each antibody is built from **four polypeptide chains** — two identical heavy chains and two
identical light chains — joined by **disulphide bridges**. The tips of the Y carry the
**variable region**, whose amino acid sequence differs from one antibody to the next and
gives each its specificity for a particular antigen. The rest, the constant region, is the
same within a class.
That variability is the whole point: the body can make millions of different antibodies, each
recognising a different foreign molecule, simply by varying the **sequence of amino acids**
in a few loops. Only a protein, with twenty different monomers to arrange, offers that much
variety — which is why antibodies could not be made of anything else.
The other options are wrong by class:
**(a) carbohydrates** are energy stores and structural materials
**(c) lipids** form membranes and store energy
**(d) enzymes** ✗ — this is the tempting one, because enzymes **are** proteins. But an enzyme
is a **catalyst**; an antibody **binds** an antigen and marks it for destruction without
catalysing any reaction. Both are proteins, but an antibody is not an enzyme.
∴ proteins.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|28|Pradeep Chemistry:
The human body **cannot synthesise vitamins** ✓ — that is precisely what makes them vitamins.
A **vitamin** is defined as an organic compound required in **small amounts** that the body
**cannot make for itself** and must therefore obtain from the **diet**. Deficiency causes a
specific disease, and supplying the vitamin cures it.
The other three the body makes continuously:
**(a) Enzymes** — synthesised from amino acids by the ribosomes, each according to its gene
**(b) DNA** — replicated in every dividing cell from nucleotide precursors
**(d) Hormones** — made by the endocrine glands: insulin in the pancreas, thyroxine in the
thyroid, adrenaline in the adrenal medulla
There are two partial exceptions worth knowing, and they do not undermine the rule:
**Vitamin D** can be made in the skin from a cholesterol derivative, but only on exposure to
**sunlight**, which is why deficiency appears where sunlight is scarce.
**Vitamin K** and some **B** vitamins are produced by the **bacteria of the large intestine**
— by the gut flora, that is, not by human cells.
Vitamins act mostly as **coenzymes**, the small non-protein partners that enzymes need to
function — so the body can make the enzyme but not the cofactor it depends on.
∴ vitamins.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|30|Pradeep Chemistry:
Continuous bleeding from a wound points to a failure of **blood clotting**, and the vitamin
required for clotting is **vitamin K** ✓ — the K standing for *Koagulation*, from the German
in which it was first described.
Vitamin K is needed for the liver to make **prothrombin** and several other clotting factors.
Without it those proteins are produced in an inactive form, the clotting cascade cannot run
to completion, and even a small injury bleeds on. Deficiency also shows as easy bruising and
bleeding gums.
It is a **fat-soluble** vitamin, found in green leafy vegetables and also made by the
**bacteria of the large intestine** — which is why dietary deficiency is rare in adults but
can appear in newborn infants, whose gut is not yet colonised. That is the reason a vitamin K
injection is given routinely at birth.
The other options cause quite different deficiency diseases:
**(a) Vitamin A** — night blindness and xerophthalmia
**(b) Vitamin E** — rare, but affects fertility and nerve function
**(c) Vitamin B₂** (riboflavin) — cheilosis, cracked lips and corners of the mouth
The same chemistry is used medically in reverse: **warfarin**, the common anticoagulant,
works by blocking vitamin K — and the antidote to a warfarin overdose is vitamin K itself.
∴ Vitamin-K.
